work.title: Passion of the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste (9 March)

paragraphs.text: March 9. The martyrdom of the forty holy martyrs who suffered martyrdom in Sebaste. In the reign of Emperor Licinius, there was a persecution of Christians. All who lived devoutly in Christ were being compelled to sacrifice to the gods, while Agricola was governor, a savage persecutor, eager to serve the devil. The Christians who were

in the army were all compelled by them to sacrifice to demons. There were soldiers from the region of Cappadocia, all of the same rank, who lived devoutly, forty in number, invincible and valiant in battle. These were their names: Dometian, Hesychius, Smaragdus, Meliton, Heraclius, Alexander, Eutychius, Lysimachus, Domnus, Sacerdon, Cyrion, Synoicus, Xanthias, Severian, Ecdicius, Acacius, John, Gaius, Athanasius, Gorgonius, Valens, Julian, Sisinnius, Philoctemon, Cyril, Valerius, Claudius, Priscus, Theodulus, Eutychius, Flavius, Leontius, Angias, Aetius, Nicholas, Chudion, Heliades, Candidus, Theophilus, Valerian. All these were arrested by the governors. They compelled them to sacrifice to demons. The governor began to say to them, “Just as you have shown success in battles and courage before your company, show your unity now as well. Together obey the emperor’s law and sacrifice to the gods before you are tortured.” But the saints said to the tormentor, “If we were victorious when fighting for a mortal emperor, as you yourself testify, how much more, when struggling for the immortal King, shall we overcome your wicked nature!”

Agricola the governor said, “One of two things lies before you: either sacrifice to the gods and retain your ranks and the honor due to you, or refuse to obey and be deprived of your lives and military service, and be handed over entirely to torture. So consider and choose what is to your advantage.” The saints said, “The Lord takes care of what is to our advantage.” The governor said, “Do not speak so much, but come forward tomorrow and sacrifice to the gods.” And he ordered them to be taken into prison. When the saints entered the prison, they bent their knees and prayed to the Lord, saying, “Deliver us, Lord, from affliction and from the snares of those who commit lawlessness.” When evening came, they began to sing this psalm: “He who lives with the help of the Most High shall dwell under the shelter of the God of heaven. He said to the Lord, ‘You are my defender and my refuge, my God; I trust in him. For he will deliver me from the hunter’s snare and from the troubling word.’” When they had finished the psalm, they prayed. Then they rose and sang again until midnight. Saint Cyrion led them in the hymns, and Saint Candidus in the responses, along with Domnus. The Savior appeared to them and said, “Your resolve is good.

But whoever endures to the end will be saved.” They all heard this voice, and in fear they remained awake until dawn. The governor summoned all his companions and ordered the saints to be brought in. The forty came and stood before the governor. The governor began to say to them, “What I am about to say, I say not to win your favor, but because it is the truth. Of all the soldiers under the emperor, none are like you: none are so brave, so wise, so handsome, or so dearly loved by me. So do not turn my love into hatred. It is up to you whether I hate or love you.” Saint Candidus said, “Your name, too, was given to you in keeping with your character, Agricolaus, for you are a savage deceiver.” The governor said, “Did I not tell you that it is up to you [?] whether I hate or love you?” Saint Candidus said, “Since it is up to us, then you, savage man, hated by God, must not choose to love us, you wicked and envious man, shrouded in darkness.” When the governor heard this, he roared like a lion and ordered them to be bound and dragged away to prison. Saint Cyrion said, “You have not received authority to torture us, but to question us.” Then the governor became afraid

and ordered them to be taken gently to prison, giving strict orders to Aglaius, the prison keeper, to guard them securely. For he was also awaiting the commander’s arrival. Throughout the day and night they received instruction from Saint Cyrion. For he said to them, “Brothers, by God’s providence we became companions in this short-lived life. So let us not be separated from one another, but just as we have lived with one soul and one mind, so let us also bear witness. Just as we have proved ourselves here to the short-lived emperor, so let us strive to be found proven before God, the great King.” After seven days had passed, while the saints were in prison, the commander arrived from Caesarea. After arriving in Sebaste, on the eighth day he sat with the governor and ordered the saints to be brought in. As they were being led in, Saint Cyrion encouraged them, saying: Brothers, let us not be afraid. For when we were in battle and prayed to God, he helped us, and we prevailed, and everyone fled. We alone, forty men, found ourselves among them. Do you remember when we fought in the great battle? With tears [?], God gave us strength, so that we [?] killed some of them and drove others away. And not a single [?] God [?] one of us was wounded by so great

a multitude. Now, then, there are three who are doing us harm: Satan, the commander, and the governor. One is invisible; is he, then, to overcome forty men? May it never be! But I beg you, let us now pray to God as we always do, and punishments, tortures, and chains will not be able to touch us. Did we not always recite this psalm whenever we began to fight: God, save me by your name, and judge me by your power. God, hear my prayer; listen to the words of my mouth. Let us recite that psalm now too, and he will hear us and help us. And as they were being led to their tormentors, they recited this psalm. Everyone gathered to watch. When they had been brought before the governor and the commander, the commander looked at them and said: These men wished to be worthy of greater honors. You will receive great honor from me, and greater gifts than others. Now let us set before you a choice between two things: either sacrifice to the gods and be considered worthy of high rank, honors, and gifts, or, if you refuse to obey, have your belts and military rank taken away and be handed over entirely to torture. Candidus said: Take both our belts and our bodies, for nothing is more precious to us than Christ.

Then the commander ordered their faces to be struck with stones. Saint Candidus said: Leader of darkness and teacher of all lawlessness, begin doing this, and you will see your punishment. Then the governor roared at the soldiers serving him and said: You wicked servants! “Why do you not quickly do what you have been commanded?” The servants picked up stones and struck one another. When the saints saw what had happened, they took courage. But the commander grew angry and picked up a stone. He threw it to strike one of the saints, but the stone turned back toward the ruler’s face and crushed his whole face. Then Saint Cyrion said, “Our enemies who fight against us have grown weak and fallen. Indeed, let their sword enter their own hearts, and let their bows be broken.” The commander said, “By the gods, some sorcery has taken place!” Saint Domnus said, “By Christ our God, he has taken vengeance! But your shameless faces speak falsely against God, for they are full of dishonor. Are you not ashamed, you dark devil of the underworld, stranger to the truth, giver of temptations? You are the devil’s head, Agricolaus, and the commander who is with you is a fox’s tail.

You are both servants of Satan. Has this first round of torture still not convinced you? Begin a second one!” The servants said to the saints, “You who are deprived of all mercy and are enemies of the gods, why do you not sacrifice to the gods?” Saint Cyrion said, “We draw near to the one God, as servants of Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit, to fulfill our resolve and complete our course through suffering, and to receive the crown of immortality, having overcome your wicked and deceitful ways.” Then the commander ordered them to be taken to prison, so that he could consider what to do about them. When they had been brought into prison, Saint Cyrion began to sing with them all, saying, “To you we have lifted our eyes, you who dwell in heaven. Look, as the eyes of servants turn to the hands of their masters, as the eyes of a maidservant turn to the hands of her mistress, so our eyes turn to the Lord our God until he has mercy on us.” After their prayer, about the sixth hour of the night, a voice came to them, and God appeared to them, saying, “Whoever believes in me, even if he dies, will live. Take courage; do not fear their tortures, for they last only a short time. Endure a little while, and suffer in accordance with the law, so that you may receive the crown.” They spent that night rejoicing in the Lord’s instruction.

When morning came, he ordered them that day to be brought out of prison and brought forward. Standing before their tormentors, they said, “Do whatever you wish.” The devil appeared, holding a sword on his right and a serpent on his left. He said into Agricolaus’s ear, “You are mine. Fight on!” Then the governor ordered them all to be bound by the neck and taken together to the lake. For there is a lake in Sebaste containing much water. At the time when the saints were being tortured, there was a severe frost. They brought them in naked and made them stand in the middle of the lake. The air was cold, and the weather was bitter. For it was toward evening. They appointed soldiers and a jailer to guard them. At the edge of the lake there was a heated bathhouse, so that anyone who wished to give in and escape could run to the bathhouse. In the first hour of the night, the saints were seized with cramps from the cold, and their flesh began to fall apart. One of the forty fell away and ran to the bathhouse. As soon as he came into contact with the warmth, he melted away, and so gave up his soul. But the saints fell down and said in a loud voice, as though with one mouth, “Are you angry with the rivers, Lord? Is your wrath against the rivers, or is your fury against the sea? For the one who separated himself

from us was poured out like water, and all his bones were scattered. But we will not turn away from you until you give us life, and we will call upon your name, which all creation praises: serpents and all the depths, fire, hail, snow, ice, and the stormy wind that carries out his word. You walk upon the sea as upon dry land and calm the savage waves with a wave of your hand. And now you are the same, Lord, who heard Moses and gave signs and wonders in Egypt, against Pharaoh and his people, dividing the sea and guiding your people in the wilderness; who heard Jacob praying as he fled from Esau’s threats; who was sold with Joseph and saved him; who heard the holy apostles. Hear us also, Lord, and do not let the raging waters drown us or the deep swallow us. For we have become utterly destitute. Help us, O God our Savior, for we stand in the depths of the sea, and our feet are wet with our own blood. Ease our burdens and the harshness of the weather, Lord our God. And let everyone know that we cried out to you and were saved.” We trusted in you and were not put to shame. And at the third hour of the night, the sun shone warmly upon them, as at harvest time.

The ice melted and became warm water. All the guards were overcome by sleep. But one gatekeeper was awake and listened to them praying. He wondered how the man who had fled to the bathhouse was not counted among the forty, but immediately melted away from the heat, while these men, despite being in such bitter cold, were still alive. And seeing the light around them, he looked up to heaven, wanting to see where the light came from. He saw crowns descending upon the heads of the saints, thirty-nine in number. And he thought to himself, saying, “There are forty of them. Why, then, is there no crown for one of them?” And realizing that the man who had fled to the bathhouse was not counted among them, he woke all the guards, stripped off his clothes, threw them in their faces, and jumped into the lake, crying out and saying, “I too am a Christian!” And going into their midst, he said, “Lord God, I believe in you, in whom these men also believed. Count me among them, and grant me also to undergo the trial of torments, so that I too may be tested.” But the devil, having been defeated, took on the form of a man. Clasping his hands and holding his knees, he said, “Woe to me! Woe to me! I have been defeated by these holy men and have become a laughingstock to everyone, having no servants of one mind with me. For if I had any,

I would not have been defeated. And now what shall I do? I will corrupt the hearts of my two rulers, and they will burn the bodies of the saints and throw them into the river. I will do this so that not even a remnant of them remains.” But Saint Cyrion said, “What god is great like our God? You are the God who works wonders. For you have turned what was against us to our advantage, and you have made up what was lacking in the forty.” And they began to sing, “Save us, Lord, for the godly man is no more.” When morning came, the two ungodly torturers arrived and found the gatekeeper sitting with them. And they asked the soldiers, “What did he see that made him do this?” The soldiers said, “We were as though dead with sleep, but he stayed awake all night. Suddenly he woke us, and we saw a great light upon them.” He immediately threw off his clothes and jumped in with them, crying out and saying, “I too am a Christian!” The two tormentors became angry and ordered them to be dragged out, bound, and taken to the seashore, and their legs to be broken with clubs. The mother of one of them stayed close by, for her son was the youngest of them all. She was afraid that he might renounce his faith, and she kept watching him, laying her hands on him and saying, “My sweet child, endure a little longer, so that you may be made perfect.

Do not be afraid, child, for Christ stands beside you, helping you.” As their shins were being broken, they gave up their souls, saying, “Our soul has escaped like a bird from the snare of the hunters. The snare was broken, and we escaped. Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.” And they all said “Amen” together and gave up their souls. But the son who had been encouraged by his mother, named Melito, was still breathing. The two tormentors ordered wagons to be brought. They loaded the bodies of the saints onto them and carried them to the riverbank, leaving the young man behind because they expected him to live. When his mother saw that he alone had been left behind, she cast aside womanly weakness and took on manly strength and wisdom. She lifted her son firmly onto her shoulder and walked behind the wagons. As his mother carried him, her son joyfully gave up his spirit. His mother, who was carrying him, laid him on top of the others. They lit a fire and burned the bodies of the saints. The two tormentors took counsel together and said, “If we leave these remains like this, the Christians will take them and fill the whole world with them. Come, let us throw them into the river.” They gathered the bones of the saints, swept up the ashes, and poured them into the river. And nothing [?]

[?] and the river [?] them. After three days they appeared to the bishop of that city, whose name was Peter, saying, “Our bones are preserved in this place. Come at night and take us out of the river.” The bishop took clergy and faithful men with him, came, and stood on the riverbank. And behold, the bones of the saints shone in the water like lamps. If a bone was left behind anywhere, it revealed itself by its light. And so, having gathered the bones of the holy martyrs, they placed them in reliquaries. And having suffered in this way, they were crowned. And they shine like stars throughout the world, having believed in God and confessed Christ. Having not rejected the Holy Spirit and having been glorified in Christ, they left a memorial in this life for the salvation of all who believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. The holy martyrs were arrested to be tortured for Christ four days before the Kalends of March, that is, on February 26. They surrendered their souls to the Lord seven days before March, under the emperor Licinius, while our Lord and God, our Savior and Master Jesus Christ, reigns over us. To him belong glory and power and honor, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
